1:#!/usr/bin/env python3
2:"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
3:their two history files, and is the only way to write them.
4:
5:An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
6:explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
7:POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
8:highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
9:nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
10:opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
11:semicolon or full stop.
12:
13:A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
14:(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
15:(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
16:`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
17:`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
18:in every entry that points to it, in the same call.
19:
20:The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
21:under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
22:UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
23:`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
24:the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
25:`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
26:`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
27:words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
28:block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).
29:
30:A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
31:the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
32:word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
33:no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
34:takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
35:that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
36:kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
37:entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
38:counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.
39:
40:Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
41:state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
42:record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
43:store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
44:open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
45:`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
46:names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
47:Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
48:history together.
49:
50:usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]
51:
52:  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
53:  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
54:  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
55:  Each write needs --from or --note.
56:
57:  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
58:      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
59:  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
60:      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
61:  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
62:                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
63:      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
64:  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
65:      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
66:  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
67:                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
68:                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
69:      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
70:      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
71:  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
72:      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
73:  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
74:      record.py check --base cc9424c2a
75:
76:An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
77:new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
78:under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:

- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.

An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:

- keep: every check passes;
- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## The pass

Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.

The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.

1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.

Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.

## How to write each entry

1. The bold title states the decision or the fact in plain words, no broader than the body.
2. Then its scope and its exact conditions. Keep every condition, exception and limit. A shorter sentence must not lose one.
3. For a position, the reason after "Why:", only if the curator gave one or accepted it in the question, or a finding in `findings.md` gives it with its ground in the team's texts, library or code. For a fact, its evidence: the test, measurement, source reading or report section, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred.
4. Keep the state apart: "Built.", or "Still to build:" in one line with where the work is tracked. Keep such lines as they are; do not move them out.
5. Name each thing. Say which call, which checker, which library, which path, when a sentence has two of them. Use no handle of a past conversation or batch ("answer 9", "ask 3", "item 48", "rung C", "decision E") unless a skill defines it.
6. **Pointers.** For each pointer (another entry, a gap-ledger row, a PLAN item, a report), decide first whether it belongs in the entry. If it stays, give it a few words on what it holds, so that a reader can decide whether to follow it without loading it. If it is only provenance, move it to the apply file's note line, where a bare reference is fine.
7. **Concepts.** Define a concept in the entry only if it belongs to this entry alone. List any other concept that a reader needs in `concepts.md` in your folder: the term, the entries that use it, and where it should be defined for every worker (the `fortress-repo` core, an area part, or the short orientation that will replace the revival part). The revival part is being rewritten: do not lean on it.
8. Do not add a claim, a reason or a scope that the sources do not hold. Do not make a claim stronger or broader. Where the sources leave the meaning open, keep the current wording for that part and write a question for the curator.
9. For a fact: keep a historical measurement only if it is stated as that measurement; move repair chronology to the history; link a count that changes at every landing to the entry that owns it. A fact may record an implementation choice made at a default; say so, and never as the curator's ruling.
10. Keep each entry near 600 characters as a check, not a cap. Clarity comes first.

Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. A coercion's body is a computation at compile time, with no method invocation: a number used as a value there converts where it stands, as a numeral does (P-173), into the type that its place fixes, and is refused statically where it does not fit, so `value object Byte(b: ZZ32)` declares `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(v)`; where nothing fixes a type, it is an exact integer, `ZZ`. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains), except two that differ only in their bounds, of which the first met is kept (row 1125). - P-174 **A numeral's type exists only at compile time: the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, below `Numeral`, with its four numbers as static parameters; every number type, the library's too, takes a numeral through a coercion generic over the four numbers.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r` and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`), so `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`; the four are naturals of any size; this implementation's `NN32` bound (P-40) is for sizes. A coercion's body is a computation at compile time, with no method invocation: a number used as a value there converts where it stands, as a numeral does (P-173), into the type that its place fixes, and is refused statically where it does not fit, so `value object Byte(b: ZZ32)` declares `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(v)`; where nothing fixes a type, it is an exact integer, `ZZ`. The coercion's body calls the type's constructor on values computed from the four numbers, as in `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Interval(roundDown(v, r, m), roundUp(v, r, m))`, and the compiler instantiates it for the numeral and folds it (P-176). No numeral value exists when a program runs: a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type, and is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. A numeral has no sign: at a program's type `-3` is the type's own prefix `-` applied to the coercion's result for `3`, and a type without `-` refuses it; any other expression of numerals alone folds first (P-173) and reaches such a type only through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`, since coercions do not chain. The design leaves out the binary chapter's numeral coercion and `opr ||` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1662`). Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations", and has libraries define the coercions into integers and rationals (`literals.tex:132-148`); the curator finishes that design, in place of the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). Row 1124 holds where the tree departs: walk loading a numeral type written as a return type, a variable's or a field's type, which it refuses only where a numeral meets it. The tree departs too, with no row, where the numeral coercions of the one library and of many tests call a getter on the four numbers, as `v.asZZ32`, and where the checker and the literals chapter read each of the four as a `ZZ` value wherever it stands (F-342, F-345).

# Cold read of `clean.txt`

Read with only `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md` and the skill's `references/` (not `revival-changes.md` or `sources.md`). Terms looked up there: the Return Type Rule and walk's load check (`interpreter.md`, "What walk checks"), the team's object-type shortcut (`interpreter.md:81`, row 697), value objects (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"), the stamp and the library order (`build-and-caches.md`), seeding (`worktrees.md`), the Working Draft (`specification.md:6`), the record's terms (`records.md`).

## 1. F-375

**Established:** Walk's check at load now applies the Return Type Rule to a pair made of a generic declaration and a plain one (no static parameters) when the plain one's domain lies inside the generic one's declared domain, even where the two parameter lists differ only at object types (where the team's old check would have called them excluding and skipped the rule). The pair loads if the plain result lies below the generic result by one of three readings, and is refused with a message naming the Return Type Rule otherwise (row 998, fixed). A tuple result is compared element by element (row 1058, fixed). Separately, `FTraitOrObject.enforceValueness` refuses a non-value type declared below a value type, and no longer refuses the symbolic type that stands for a type parameter (row 997, fixed).

**Conditions:** Walk only, at load, generic-beside-plain pairs. Limits: a plain declaration that writes no return type is not judged (row 1044); `comprises` clauses are not read; two plain declarations still get the team's shortcut (row 697). Since the five number types were merged with their objects (P-178, F-379), every generic-beside-plain pair over them goes through the declared-domain reading. Three of the choices (no `comprises` reading, no judgment without a return type, the value check and its "both directions" repair, the three readings) were made by the coordinator, the planner or a worker; the curator decided none.

**Consequence:** A worker should write the return type on a plain overload beside a generic one (otherwise the rule is silently skipped), should expect a pair over object types that breaks the rule to be refused at load now, and should treat the listed choices as open, not as the curator's decisions (if one matters to the work, that is a reason to explore). No walk test changed between loading and refusing, and no expected-failure test changed kind.

**Evidence:** The seven named tests under `ProjectFortress/tests/`; the suite result stated (every pair loaded before still loads); old-against-new runs in the three cited reports.

**Could not resolve:**
- "an own generic's declared domain": unclear wording. I read it as "a generic declaration of the same name"; it could also mean "a declaration with static parameters of its own" (F-26's term).
- "by one of three readings that the report gives": the entry does not say what the three readings are, nor at which instance "the generic's" result is taken. So I cannot tell from the entry which pairs load. Not standing alone.
- "a `comprises` clause is not read (row 550's pair at `ZZ64`, fixed since `ZZ64` is an object, F-379)": two readings. Either row 550 is an example of the limitation that no longer bites because `ZZ64` stopped needing a `comprises` clause, or row 550 is where `comprises` reading was fixed. I took the first; the wording does not settle it.
- "the repair of both directions in one step": unclear wording. Both directions of what: of the value check (refusing a non-value below a value type, and passing a type parameter), or of the Return Type Rule (loading and refusing)?
- "the five number types merged with their objects": a history/language concept I lack. The skill says the number types other than `QQ` are object types (`interpreter.md:78`) and that the prelude has seven number types each one `value object` (`compiler.md:34`); neither says which five, or what they were merged from.
- "passes the symbolic type of a type parameter": where such a type meets the value check is not said; the test names (`...ValueBoundWalk`) suggest a type parameter bounded by a value type. Unclear wording.
- "the coordinator", "the batch's planner": roles the skill does not define; only their consequence (not the curator) matters, and that is clear.
- Conflict with the skill: `interpreter.md:80` still says walk refuses row 1058's valid tuple pair, which this entry says is fixed. A worker reading both meets two contrary statements.

## 2. F-403

**Established:** The one library declares `EQV` (`≡`) and `NEQV` (`≢`) on two `Boolean`s as top-level operators next to `<->`. `EQV` is `if a then b else NOT b end` (deliberately avoiding `=`, which row 994 concerns on the compiled path), and `NEQV` is `NOT (a EQV b)`, as the specification defines `≢`. Both paths run them under the one library. Applied to two objects of a program's own type they are type errors: walk stops at the call with a unification error, the compiled checker refuses the call.

**Conditions:** One library, both paths. The specification and the prelude make them methods of `Boolean`; the one library keeps top-level operators for its boolean operators. With `AplCore` imported, its infix `≡` and prefix `≢` over `RR64` and arrays share an overload set with the library's two: its calls give what they gave before, and booleans get the library's answers (`t ≡ f` is `false`, `t ≢ f` is `true`). No gated program and no microGPT line imports `AplCore`. Limits: an undeclared equivalence operator such as `APPROX` still loads under walk and fails at the call with an internal error (row 1118); `⊕`, `⊼`, `⊽` and `majority` are not declared (row 1121).

**Consequence:** A worker can use `≡`/`≢` on booleans under the one library on both paths, should not expect them to work on other types, and should know that the top-level form and the merge with `AplCore` are plan defaults the curator has not decided. Avoid `=` on two booleans in compiled code (row 994).

**Evidence:** `tests/BooleanEquivalenceWalk.fss`, `one_library_tests/OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence.test`; the quoted error messages; the cited report sections.

**Could not resolve:**
- "within P-37, a default of the batch's plan that the curator has not decided": two readings. Since a P- entry is a curator's decision (`records.md`), I read it as "the top-level form fits within P-37, and is itself a plan default"; read literally, it says P-37 is undecided.
- "This also is the plan's default, not decided by the curator": unclear what "this" is: the merging with `AplCore`'s operators into one overload set, or the absence of any conflict handling, or the fact that nothing gated imports `AplCore`.
- "(row 994 is `=` of two booleans, compiled)": telegraphic. I read it as "row 994 is an open defect of `=` on two booleans on the compiled path", but the entry does not say the row is open or what the defect is.
- "an equivalence operator that nothing declares": a language concept (the specification's class of equivalence operators) not in the skill; the example `APPROX` lets me guess.
- "its own form for the boolean operators": inferred as "top-level operators rather than methods of `Boolean`" from the contrast; not stated.

## 3. F-404

**Established:** `seed-worktree.sh` copies `ProjectFortress/build` but not `ProjectFortress/build-one`. The implementation stamp covers `build-one` too. So when the base build has a `build-one`, the seeded worktree's stamp check fails at the first `ant` target: it prints 'Sources and build as the last build left them? no', rebuilds the Scala, and empties both `caches` and `caches-one`. Before that first build, a compiled run with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` fails with 'java.lang.Error: The type ZZ of the library that the compiled path reads is not compiled over ... FZZ ...'.

**Conditions:** Only for a worktree seeded from a base build that has `build-one`. Holds until the script is changed.

**Consequence:** A seeded worker must budget a Scala build plus the library order before the first compiled run, and should not trust a compiled one-library run in a freshly seeded worktree before building. The skill's promise that a seeded worktree "runs walk and the compiled path right away" and that `ant compileAll` "keeps the seeded caches" (`worktrees.md:36`, `:45`) does not hold in this case.

**Evidence:** `build.xml:400-402`, `:469-470` (the stamp), `seed-worktree.sh:86-93` (the copy); no test, but the command `cd ProjectFortress && FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ../bin/fortress run OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence` exits 1 with the error, in a fresh seeded worktree; report section "Defects, and their homes".

**Could not resolve:**
- `build-one`: not defined anywhere I may read. I guess it is a build output for the one library's runtime, but I cannot say what it holds or when a base build has one. Concept I lack (the skill mentions only `ProjectFortress/build`).
- "a compiled run under `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` before it stops, '...'": garden-path wording. I read "before it" as "before that first build", and "stops" as the verb; it could be misread as "before it stops".
- Whether a compiled run without the variable, or a walk run, also fails before the first build is not said.
- Whether the defect has a ledger row, or is to be fixed in the script, is not said ("No test" only).

## 4. F-405

**Established:** Under walk, a trait or object can declare several generic dotted methods of one name, and walk runs them. The object builds each generic method as one symbolic instance, keyed by the method's name and the kinds of its static parameters; an object's redeclaration of a trait's generic method thus replaces it. A call without static arguments infers them and dispatches among the instances; a call with static arguments instantiates each method whose static parameters (number and kinds) accept them, then chooses by the arguments as for a top-level generic function.

**Conditions:** Walk only, dotted generic methods. Limits: two methods of the same arity whose static parameters differ only in bounds collapse into one instance and the first met is kept, so a call can silently run the less specific one (row 1125: `Nested.tk(n)` on a `ZZ32` answers 2 from `tk[\U extends Number\]` instead of 3 from `tk[\U extends ZZ32\]`). A call on a receiver "assumed at the trait" stops (row 1126). A plain and a generic method of one name: a call with static arguments stops (row 744). Of two generic functional methods of one name and arity, the second is never chosen (row 1123).

**Consequence:** A worker can overload generic dotted methods by arity and by static-parameter kinds under walk, but must not overload them only by bounds, must not mix a plain and a generic method of one name where calls write static arguments, and must not rely on the second of two same-arity generic functional methods.

**Evidence:** The first-met rule was read in the code; row 1125 was observed; tests `tests/GenericMethodOverloadArity.fss`, `GenericMethodOverloadSetWalk.fss`, `GenericOverloadStaticArgKindsWalk.fss`; the cited report sections and `SKEPTIC.md`.

**Could not resolve:**
- "one symbolic instantiation for each name and kinds of static parameters" against "Two such methods of one number of parameters ... share that instantiation": unclear whether the number of value parameters is part of the key. If it is not, two methods of different arities with the same static-parameter kinds would collide, which the arity test suggests they do not.
- "the first met is kept": first in source order, in inheritance order, or in a hash order? Not said.
- "A call on a receiver assumed at the trait stops (row 1126)": unclear wording. Walk has no static types, so I cannot tell what "assumed at the trait" means (a call on `self` in the trait's body? a receiver bound through a trait-typed variable?), nor with what error it stops.
- Conflict with the skill: `interpreter.md:82` says two generic dotted methods that differ in arity load and a call fails (row 1057). This entry's title and its `GenericMethodOverloadArity.fss` test suggest that is fixed, but the entry does not name row 1057.

## 5. F-406

**Established:** On the compiled path, a setter call `c.t := v` (a method call after the desugarer) now passes `v` at the setter's parameter type for the receiver's instance, including when the receiver is typed by a type variable whose bounds have the setter (with a cast when it has `self`'s type, F-377). When the checker leaves a call with several candidate declarations, the code generator now writes into the class the overload (dispatch) method that the call names, and, where the call's signature differs from the overload set's principal member, a forwarding method at the call's signature. So setter assignments at a narrower value, `s.r := self` at a listed type, `num(R)` beside a trait's `num(self)`, calls on `self` in such a trait, and calls that one declaration takes directly and another by coercion all compile and run; the one library's `FortressLibrary` now holds `numerator{...}` and `denominator{...}`.

**Conditions:** Compiled path. The written overload method is a plan default and the forwarder a worker's choice; the alternative was routing each call through the trait; the curator has decided neither. Limit: the checker still refuses a comprised object's functional method declared at a narrower return type (row 1127).

**Consequence:** A worker can rely on these call forms compiling, should treat the generated overload method and forwarder as provisional designs, and should not write a narrower return type on a comprised object's functional method.

**Evidence:** `compiler_tests/VarFieldAssignedSubtypeRun`, `FunctionalMethodComprisedObject`, `ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall`, `CoercionAnyOverloadRungC`; the named `CodeGen` methods; report sections 1 and 5.

**Could not resolve:**
- "an arrowless call after the desugarer", "the call's arrow": compiled-path concept I lack. I guess the arrow is the function type the checker attaches to a call, and the desugared setter call has none, but the skill does not say.
- "its set split with its principal member": unclear wording and an undefined concept. I cannot tell what "principal member" is (the most general declaration? the first?) or what splitting the set means.
- "cast below self's trait where it has self's type (F-377)": unclear which value is cast to what, and what "has self's type" means here.
- "`s.r := self` at a listed type": I guess "listed" means listed in a `comprises` clause; not said.
- "`numerator{...}` and `denominator{...}`": notation I cannot read (generated method names? overload-set names?), and why it matters is not said.
